name: The Consequence Argument
statement: If our acts follow from the fixed past and laws, and those aren't up to us, neither are our acts.
meaning: The Consequence Argument is the most influential argument for incompatibilism, the thesis that free will is incompatible with determinism. It is most associated with Peter van Inwagen, who developed it in his 1983 book An Essay on Free Will, though similar arguments were given earlier by Carl Ginet and David Wiggins. In its intuitive form, van Inwagen states it as follows: if determinism is true, then our acts are the consequences of the laws of nature and events in the remote past, but it is not up to us what went on before we were born, and neither is it up to us what the laws of nature are, therefore the consequences of these things, including our present acts, are not up to us. The argument turns on two claims of fixity, the fixity of the past and the fixity of the laws, neither of which is within our power, together with a transfer principle: if we have no choice about some fact, and no choice about the fact that it implies a further fact, then we have no choice about that further fact. Van Inwagen expressed this with an operator, often written N, meaning that a proposition is true and no one has or ever had any choice about it, and the transfer principle is often called Rule Beta. If sound, the argument shows that if determinism is true we have no choice about our own actions, and hence no free will. It is the central modern argument that free will requires the falsity of determinism.
mechanism: The Consequence Argument reasons from the fixity of the past and the laws to the fixity of our present actions. Suppose determinism is true. Then the complete state of the world in the remote past, before anyone now living was born, together with the laws of nature, logically entails everything that happens now, including what I do at this moment. Now consider two facts about which no one has any choice: the state of the remote past, which is over and done with and was settled before we existed, and the laws of nature, which we are powerless to alter. The argument then invokes a principle of transfer of powerlessness: if no one has any choice about a fact P, and no one has any choice about the fact that P implies Q, then no one has any choice about Q. Applying this, since we have no choice about the past-and-laws, and, given determinism, no choice about the fact that the past-and-laws entail our present acts, it follows that we have no choice about our present acts. Van Inwagen formalized this using the N operator, where NP means that P is true and no one has, or ever had, any choice about whether P, and gave three versions of the argument; the transfer inference from NP and N(P implies Q) to NQ is the controversial Rule Beta. Because having free will seems to require having a choice about what one does, the conclusion that we have no choice about our acts, if determinism holds, yields incompatibilism. The whole force of the argument thus rests on the two fixity claims and on the validity of the transfer principle.

examples.text: Our acts follow from the remote past and the laws; we have no choice about those, so we have no choice about our acts.
The argument leans on the fixity of the past, settled before we were born, and the fixity of the unchangeable laws.
Rule Beta transfers powerlessness: no choice about P, and none about P implying Q, means no choice about Q.

whyItMatters: The Consequence Argument is the centerpiece of the modern free will debate and the most powerful and precise statement of the case for incompatibilism. Before van Inwagen's formulation, the claim that free will requires the falsity of determinism often rested on vague intuitions; the Consequence Argument turned it into a rigorous argument with clearly stated premises about the fixity of the past and the laws and an explicit transfer principle, forcing compatibilists to say exactly where they get off. Its influence has been enormous: much of the contemporary literature on free will consists of attempts either to defend or to rebut it, and it reframed the whole dispute around the notions of powerlessness, the fixity of the past, and what it is for something to be up to us. Compatibilist responses to it, such as David Lewis's local-miracle compatibilism and the demonstration by Thomas McKay and David Johnson that the transfer principle Rule Beta is invalid, are themselves landmarks of the field. By articulating so sharply why a determined agent might seem to have no choice about anything they do, the argument crystallizes the deepest worry about reconciling freedom with a law-governed world.

working.text: suppose the remote past and the laws together entail everything we now do.
observe that we have no choice about the remote past or about the laws of nature.
conclude, via the transfer principle, that we have no choice about our present acts either.

limits: The Consequence Argument is powerful but not decisive, and compatibilists have mounted serious replies to each of its moving parts. The most technical target is the transfer principle. Thomas McKay and David Johnson showed in 1996 that the inference rule van Inwagen called Beta is invalid, because it entails a further principle of agglomeration, from having no choice about P and no choice about Q to having no choice about their conjunction, that admits counterexamples; this forced van Inwagen and others to seek repaired versions of the principle. A different response attacks the fixity of the laws: David Lewis, in his 1981 paper Are We Free to Break the Laws?, defended local-miracle compatibilism, distinguishing a weak sense in which an agent is able to do something such that, if they did it, a law would have been broken, from a strong and incredible sense in which the agent would themselves break a law, and arguing that free agents have only the harmless weak ability. Still other compatibilists question the fixity of the past or the dependence relations involved. Some datings and journal details, such as van Inwagen 1983, Lewis 1981, and McKay and Johnson 1996, and the exact wording of the argument, reward care.
misreadings: The Consequence Argument does not assume that determinism is true; it argues conditionally that if determinism holds, we lack free will. It is not the claim that our acts are uncaused or that we do nothing, but that, given determinism, we have no choice about what we do. And its conclusion is contested, since compatibilists challenge the transfer principle and the fixity of the laws, so treating the argument as asserting determinism, as denying that we act, or as an uncontested proof, misreads it.
origin: Peter van Inwagen's argument, in An Essay on Free Will (1983) and anticipated by Ginet and Wiggins, that if determinism is true our acts are consequences of the fixed past and laws, which are not up to us, so our acts are not up to us either.
